sentences.text: Citipati was among the largest oviraptorids, measuring between 2.5 and 2.9 meters in length and weighing 75 to 110 kilograms.
This animal possessed toothless upper and lower jaws that terminated in a horny beak.
Its tail ended in a pygostyle, a fused structure of the final caudal vertebrae that supported large tail feathers.
Unlike most other theropods, Citipati possessed an unusually long neck and a shortened tail.
Remains were first collected in the 1990s at the Ukhaa Tolgod locality within the Djadochta Formation.

A small fossilized oviraptorid embryo was discovered in 1993 at the Ukhaa Tolgod locality in the Gobi Desert during a joint expedition by the Mongolian Academy of Sciences and the American Museum of Natural History.
In 2001, James M. Clark, Mark A. Norell, and Rinchen Barsbold named Citipati osmolskae based on holotype IGM 100/978 and referred specimens IGM 100/971 and IGM 100/979 to the genus.
The generic name Citipati is derived from Sanskrit words meaning funeral pyre lord, referencing a figure in Tibetan Buddhism folklore.
Citipati had long feathers on its arms and tail, which may have protected eggs and young from the elements.
A 2022 study estimated Citipati's bite force to be between 349.3 N and 499.0 N.
Citipati likely fed on tougher vegetation than other herbivorous theropods in its environment.
In 2020, Gregory F. Funston and colleagues established the new subfamily Citipatiinae to separate Citipati from Oviraptor.
Citipati lived approximately 71 to 75 million years ago during the Late Cretaceous period.
Citipati inhabited arid to semiarid environments consisting of large sand dunes and short-lived water bodies.
At least four specimens of Citipati have been found in nesting positions, including the famous specimen known as Big Momma.
It is debated whether remains from the nearby Zamyn Khondt locality represent a second species of Citipati.
Researchers debated whether the Zamyn Khondt oviraptorid specimen represents a second species of Citipati.
It is debated whether juvenile troodontid skulls found near Citipati nests were prey, nest raiders, or evidence of nest parasitism.
It is debated whether the IGN specimen represents a second species of Citipati or a completely distinct genus.
